categories.skills: Skills and plugins for coding agents
categories.framework: Agent frameworks and official MCP catalogs

entries.name: .NET Agent Skills (official)
entries.what: The .NET team's curated skills and custom agents for coding agents: plugins for general .NET, data access/EF, diagnostics, MSBuild, NuGet, upgrades and MAUI.
entries.reason: First-party, MIT, and actively pushed. The README links a public dashboard comparing token use and pass rates per skill, which is rare. Caveat: the agent files follow GitHub Copilot conventions and the README says they are not installed as native Codex agents.
entries.pick_if: you want a baseline set of .NET skills from the people who ship the SDK.

entries.name: dotnet-skills (community)
entries.what: A Claude Code / Codex plugin with 30 skills and 5 agents (per its README) covering C#, Akka.NET, Aspire, EF Core, testing and performance.
entries.reason: MIT, recently pushed, and installs as a Claude Code plugin marketplace. Caveat: opinionated and partly Akka.NET-centric; read the skills you enable instead of installing everything.
entries.pick_if: you want community patterns that complement the official skills, especially if you use Akka.NET or Aspire.

entries.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
entries.what: Microsoft's open framework for building agents and multi-agent workflows in .NET and Python (the README also points to a separate Go SDK).
entries.reason: First-party, MIT, and releasing often (dotnet-1.28.0 on 2026-11-06). Caveat: the pace and the open-issue count are both high, so pin versions and read release notes before upgrading.
entries.pick_if: you are building your own agents on .NET and want the vendor-supported route.

entries.name: Microsoft MCP servers (Azure, Fabric)
entries.what: The source repo for Microsoft's official MCP servers; its README lists the Azure MCP server and the Microsoft Fabric MCP server.
entries.reason: First-party, MIT, active, C#. Caveat: it is a contributor repo, so start from each server's own README (linked from the table) rather than building from source.
entries.pick_if: your agent needs to work with Azure resources or Fabric.

entries.name: apra-fleet
entries.what: Coordinates coding agents across several of your own machines (README: devices, providers and workflows), with credentials, health checks and a sprint dashboard.
entries.reason: Active and ambitious, and the README says the repo is built by the product itself. Caveats: GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION although the LICENSE file contains Apache-2.0 text, the README's scale claims are not independently verified here, and I did not run it.
entries.pick_if: you already run agents on more than one machine and want an orchestrator to trial.
entries.license_note: LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 text; GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION

entries.name: fleet (fleetSpark)
entries.what: Runs agents across your own machines, coordinated through git branches rather than SSH; works with Claude Code, Codex, Aider or A2A agents per its README.
entries.reason: MIT and an appealing design (git as the bus), but very small (3 stars) and the last push is months old. Fine to follow, too early to depend on.
entries.pick_if: you want a git-only, no-infrastructure way to fan work out to a few machines and can tolerate a young tool.

entries.name: RoslynMCP (carquiza)
entries.what: C# code-analysis MCP server on Roslyn: wildcard symbol search, reference tracking, dependency and complexity analysis.
entries.reason: No license detected (so default copyright applies), no push since 2025-06-24, and the README targets .NET 8 and Claude Desktop only. Was the most-starred Roslyn MCP when checked, but stars do not offset a year-plus of silence.
entries.pick_if: never for new work; read it only for ideas.

entries.name: RoslynMcpServer (JoshuaRamirez)
entries.what: Roslyn MCP server focused on refactoring: 66 tools claimed in the README, preview mode on every operation, atomic writes with rollback.
entries.reason: MIT, very active, installs as a dotnet tool. Caveats: it rewrites your source, so use preview and a clean git tree; the open-issue count (about 2,300) is far above its size and is not a reliable bug signal; the 66-tool surface is large for an agent to choose from.
entries.pick_if: you want automated refactoring (rename, move, extract) and will review the diffs.

entries.name: RoslynMcp (MadQ)
entries.what: Roslyn MCP server for C# code intelligence: type resolution, cross-file references, semantic rename with preview/apply, diagnostics. 46 tools (44 public, 2 debug-only) per its README.
entries.reason: MIT, active, documents its security boundary (file access limited to the workspace tree) and ships setup for common MCP clients. Caveats: self-described beta, installs with --prerelease, requires the .NET 10 or 11 SDK, and a recent breaking rename of the package and tool key. Self-described beta; not yet hands-on tested here, so watch rather than use.
entries.pick_if: you want one Roslyn server for navigation plus careful rename, and you are on a current SDK.

entries.name: RoslynMcpExtension (sailro)
entries.what: A Visual Studio extension that exposes the live Visual Studio Roslyn workspace over MCP: validate file, find references, go to definition, symbol search, dead-code search.
entries.reason: MIT. Its edge is seeing unsaved changes and live diagnostics. Caveats: Visual Studio 2022/2026 only, built from source per the README, 7 read-only tools, last push 2026-04-11.
entries.pick_if: you work inside Visual Studio and want the agent to see what the IDE sees.

entries.name: roslyn-mcp (egorpavlikhin)
entries.what: Minimal Roslyn MCP server with two tools: ValidateFile and FindUsages.
entries.reason: No license detected, no push since 2025-05-15, no packaged install (run from a local project path).
entries.pick_if: never for new work.

entries.name: RoslynMcp (chrismo80)
entries.what: Roslyn MCP server built around load solution/project/type/member, reference search and call-graph tracing; uses Roslynator (Apache-2.0).
entries.reason: MIT, a dotnet tool on NuGet, .NET 10. Small (13 stars) and last pushed 2026-05-19. Reasonable to try; I would not standardize a team on it yet.
entries.pick_if: you want a lightweight, read-oriented Roslyn server and like the call-graph workflow.

entries.name: mssql_mcp_server (RichardHan)
entries.what: Python MCP server for SQL Server: list tables and run queries, read-only by default with an optional write mode; SQL, Windows and Azure AD auth; LocalDB and Azure SQL.
entries.reason: MIT, the most-starred of the group, and the safest default (read-only unless you opt in). Caveats: the README example puts the password in the client config env block, and it is Python, so it needs uv/Python next to a .NET toolchain.
entries.pick_if: you want agents to read from SQL Server with a safe default and do not need DBA diagnostics.

entries.name: mssql-mcp (Aaronontheweb)
entries.what: C# MCP server for SQL Server with three tools: execute_sql, list_tables, list_schemas. Runs in Docker or as a .NET app.
entries.reason: Apache-2.0 and native .NET. Caveats: execute_sql accepts any statement including INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and DDL, and the README handles safety by advising a SELECT-only database login, not by a server-side switch. Last push 2026-01-22.
entries.pick_if: you want a .NET-native server and will connect it with a least-privilege login.

facts.writes: unrestricted by server (use a read-only login)

entries.name: MCPSqlServer (ian-cowley)
entries.what: Standalone C# SQL Server MCP server: schema exploration, query and stored-procedure execution, and a resolver that swaps connection strings based on the active editor file.
entries.reason: MIT, .NET 10, no open issues. Caveats: it can execute stored procedures and queries, the setup keeps credentials in appsettings.json, and it is small (19 stars).
entries.pick_if: you want editor-aware connection switching and accept a young project.

entries.name: sql-mcp-server (nocentino)
entries.what: A SQL Server 2025 demo comparing two patterns: Data API Builder as a zero-code MCP server for app data, and a custom TypeScript server with 34 DMV-based DBA tools (blocking, waits, missing indexes, backups).
entries.reason: Excellent explanation of when to use which pattern, and result sets are capped with a truncated flag. Caveat: no license is detected, so you cannot safely reuse the code, and it is a Docker Compose demo rather than a drop-in tool.
entries.pick_if: you want to learn what a DBA-oriented MCP server should expose, or compare it with Data API Builder.

entries.name: TSQLLint
entries.what: Configurable linter for T-SQL anti-patterns; installs as a dotnet tool, Homebrew formula or npm package.
entries.reason: MIT, T-SQL specific, easy to put in CI. Caveat: the latest GitHub release is 1.16.0 from 2024-09-19 even though the repo was pushed in 2026-08, so check you are getting what you expect.
entries.pick_if: you want a T-SQL-only linter in CI or as a gate for agent-written SQL.

entries.name: SQLFluff
entries.what: Dialect-flexible SQL linter and auto-formatter; its README lists T-SQL among the supported dialects.
entries.reason: MIT, very active, large community. Caveats: it is Python, and T-SQL coverage depends on its dialect grammar, so test it on your own scripts before enforcing it.
entries.pick_if: you also have non-T-SQL SQL, or want auto-formatting as well as linting.

entries.name: tsqlscope
entries.what: A newer T-SQL linter with diagnostics, simple configuration and fixes it labels safe; documented per 0.1 release line.
entries.reason: MIT and well-documented for its age, but 2 stars and a 0.1 line. Worth following, not yet worth depending on.
entries.pick_if: you want auto-fix for T-SQL and are willing to track a young tool.

entries.name: sqlskim (archived)
entries.what: A T-SQL linter and database verifier from Microsoft.
entries.reason: Archived, last pushed 2022-11-28, a two-line README, and no license detected by GitHub. Listed so you do not adopt it by accident.
entries.pick_if: never; use TSQLLint or SQLFluff.

entries.name: awesome-claude-code-plugins
entries.what: A broad list of Claude Code plugins, slash commands, subagents, MCP servers and hooks, grouped by theme.
entries.reason: Apache-2.0 and a handy browse source, but general rather than .NET-focused, last pushed 2026-08-12, and the list does not say what was verified per entry. Treat items as leads to check.
entries.pick_if: you want to browse for non-.NET Claude Code add-ons.

entries.name: best-of-mcp-servers
entries.what: A ranked list of MCP servers (410 projects in 34 categories per its README), regenerated weekly.
entries.reason: Good for discovery across all of MCP. Caveats: ranking is a computed score, not a review; it is not .NET or SQL Server specific; its content is CC-BY-SA-4.0, so do not copy it into other repos without attribution and share-alike.
entries.pick_if: you want to scan the wider MCP field before narrowing to .NET.
